sections.heading: A resolver follows the delegation to the name servers of your hosted zone

plan.problem: A user types www.example.com. The browser needs an IP address, and no single server holds every name on the internet.
trace: **Ask the resolver.** The browser asks a DNS resolver, [typically managed by the user's internet service provider] (route53-resolver-typically-managed-by-isp), [also known as a recursive name server] (route53-dns-resolver-is-recursive-name-server).

**Follow the delegation.** The resolver asks [a sequence of authoritative DNS name servers] (route53-dns-resolver-is-recursive-name-server). The TLD name server for .com answers with the [names of the four Route 53 name servers] (route53-tld-returns-four-name-servers) of the domain.

**Ask the authority.** A Route 53 name server has [definitive information about one part] of DNS (route53-authoritative-ns-definition). It looks in the [example.com hosted zone for the www.example.com record] and [returns the IP address to the DNS resolver] (route53-name-server-returns-value-from-hosted-zone).
**Cache.** The resolver gives the address to the browser and keeps it; the name servers are typically [cached for two days] (route53-resolver-caches-ns-two-days).
plan.table: Who holds what (columns: Part | Who runs it | What it holds): DNS resolver | the internet service provider or the company network | answers it has cached; TLD name server for .com | the TLD operator | the four Route 53 name servers of example.com; Route 53 name server | AWS | the hosted zone, [A container for records] (route53-hosted-zone-container); registrar | the company where the name is registered | which name servers the domain uses ([update the name servers for your domain], route53-faq-external-registrar-must-update-name-servers).
plan.why: Why a chain of servers? Each level points to the next, so the owner of a zone controls its own records: Route 53 name servers [store the hosted zones] (route53-authoritative-ns-for-route53-domains) of the domains that use them, and nobody else has to.
plan.exam_signal: "use Route 53 for DNS but keep the domain at the current registrar" points to a public hosted zone and new name servers at the registrar; a transfer [isn't required to use other Route 53 features] (route53-domain-transfer-not-required-for-other-features). "register the domain with AWS" points to Route 53 domain registration, which [makes itself the DNS service for the domain] (route53-domain-registration-makes-route53-the-dns-service).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: subdomains, twin zones and global answers. You can [create a separate hosted zone for a subdomain] and delegate it by [creating another NS record in the hosted zone] of the parent (route53-ns-record-delegates-subdomain); [always delegate from the parent zone] (route53-delegate-from-immediate-parent-zone). A separate zone lets you [use IAM permissions to restrict access] (route53-subdomain-delegation-limits-access-by-iam). Two zones can share one name; Route 53 [never returns values for records] of the other zone (route53-same-name-zones-never-mix-records). Answers come from a [global anycast network of DNS servers] (route53-faq-global-anycast-low-latency). At most 80 words.
plan.body_extras: One sentence in the trace or after the table: each new hosted zone gets [a unique set of four name servers] (route53-default-unique-delegation-set-per-zone), listed in the NS record that Route 53 creates with the SOA record ([a start of authority (SOA) record], route53-zone-creates-ns-and-soa).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the resolver finds your name servers through the TLD, then asks Route 53. The thing to watch is the registrar, which must list your hosted zone's name servers.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company creates a public hosted zone for example.com in Route 53 and copies all its records into it. The registrar still lists the old DNS provider's name servers. Which name servers answer the users' queries? Answer: the old provider's; Route 53 [will not be authoritative for queries] (route53-faq-registrar-must-use-hosted-zone-name-servers) until the registrar uses the zone's name servers.

sections.heading: The record type decides what kind of value a name returns

plan.problem: One domain needs the address of a web server, the name of a mail server and a text value that proves ownership. One kind of record cannot hold all three.
trace: **Name and type.** A record is [an object in a hosted zone] that says [how you want to route traffic] (route53-record-defined); the [record type usually determines the type of resource] (route53-record-type-determines-resource-type).
**Addresses.** An A record routes [using an IPv4 address] (route53-a-record-ipv4) and an AAAA record [using an IPv6 address] (route53-aaaa-record-ipv6).
**Names.** A CNAME record maps [queries for the name of the current record] [to another domain] (route53-cname-record-maps-name-to-name).
**Policy and TTL.** For each record you [choose a routing policy] (route53-routing-policy-determines-response), and every record [must have a TTL] (route53-ttl-required-on-all-records).
plan.table: Record types you meet in questions (columns: Type | Value | Typical use): A | IPv4 address | web server; AAAA | IPv6 address | web server on IPv6; CNAME | another domain name | www to a name outside the zone; MX | [specifies the names of your mail servers] (route53-mx-record-mail-servers-priority) | email; NS | [identifies the name servers for the hosted zone] (route53-ns-record-identifies-name-servers) | delegation; TXT | [strings that are enclosed in double quotation marks] (route53-txt-record-strings) | ownership proofs; CAA | which [certificate authorities (CAs) are allowed to issue certificates] (route53-caa-record-purpose) | certificate control.
plan.why: Why types? A resolver asks for one name and one type, so each client gets the kind of value it needs: a browser an address, a mail server a mail host.
plan.exam_signal: "route a name to an EC2 instance whose address must not change" points to an A record with an Elastic IP address, which [will never change] (route53-ec2-elastic-ip-recommended); "several addresses for one name" fits one simple record: you can list [multiple IP addresses for an A record] (route53-faq-a-record-multiple-ip-addresses).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: a CNAME record takes one value ([For all types except CNAME] you can enter more than one, route53-cname-record-takes-one-value-only), and with a CNAME record for a name you [cannot create any other records for that subdomain] (route53-cname-excludes-other-records-same-name).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the record type tells the resolver what kind of value comes back. The thing to watch is a CNAME record, which leaves no room for other records of that name.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team releases the Elastic IP address of a retired web server but keeps the A record old.example.com. What is the risk? Answer: a [dangling DNS record that can be taken over] by whoever gets the address next; you must [also delete the DNS record pointing to it] (route53-released-elastic-ip-delete-dns-record-dangling).

sections.heading: An alias record can answer at the zone apex where a CNAME record cannot

plan.problem: A company wants example.com, with no www, to open its website behind a load balancer. The load balancer has a DNS name, not a fixed address.
trace: **Name the apex.** example.com is the zone apex, [the top node of a DNS namespace] (route53-alias-allowed-at-zone-apex).
**Try a CNAME record.** The [DNS protocol does not allow you to create] a CNAME record there (route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex); CNAME records work for names such as www.example.com.

**Use an alias record.** An alias record is an [Amazon Route 53-specific extension to DNS] (route53-faq-alias-is-route53-extension) with the [type of A or AAAA] (route53-faq-alias-type-a-or-aaaa-like-cname), and [you can create an alias record] at the apex (route53-alias-allowed-at-zone-apex).

**Answer directly.** Route 53 returns the target's addresses itself; it [responds to a DNS query only when] the name and type match the alias record (route53-alias-answers-only-on-matching-name-and-type).
plan.table: Alias record or CNAME record (columns: Question | Alias record | CNAME record): at the zone apex | yes | no; target | [route traffic to selected AWS resources], or [one record in a hosted zone to another] (route53-alias-extension-targets) | any name: it [can redirect DNS queries to any DNS record] (route53-alias-targets-only-selected-aws-resources); queries to an AWS resource | [do not incur a charge] (route53-pricing-alias-free-for-listed-aws-services) | Route 53 [charges for CNAME queries] (route53-alias-queries-free-cname-charged); TTL | [Route 53 uses the default TTL for the resource] (route53-alias-to-aws-resource-ttl-not-settable) | you set it.
plan.why: Why does AWS offer its own record type? A CNAME record sends the resolver to ask again, which [increases latency and costs]; an alias record gives a direct answer (route53-best-practice-alias-cheaper-faster-than-cname).
plan.exam_signal: "point the zone apex to a load balancer, a CloudFront distribution or an S3 website" points to an alias record, which works [both for the root domain] and for subdomains (route53-cname-only-for-subdomains); "a subdomain that points to a host name outside AWS" points to a CNAME record, because [You don't need to use Route 53 as the DNS service] for the target (route53-cname-target-need-not-be-route53).
plan.try_it: route53-t02: one 'Try it' callout after the Exam signal.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: at the bare domain, use an alias record, because a CNAME record is not allowed there. The thing to watch is the target, which must be an AWS resource or a record in the zone.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team wants blog.example.com to open a blog that a hosting company runs at blog.hostingco.net, outside AWS. It tries an alias record. Does Route 53 accept it, and what should the team use? Answer: no; an alias record [can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources] (route53-alias-targets-only-selected-aws-resources) or to a record in the same zone; blog.example.com is a subdomain, so a CNAME record works.

sections.heading: An alias record follows the changing addresses of the AWS resource it names

plan.problem: A load balancer has no fixed IP address. As it scales, its addresses change, so a record that holds today's addresses breaks later.
trace: **The resource changes.** Elastic Load Balancing scales the [load balancer and updates the DNS entry] (route53-elb-dns-entry-updated-ttl-60), whose [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds] lets the [IP addresses can be remapped quickly] (elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap).
**The record names the resource.** The alias record holds the load balancer, not its addresses: [An Elastic Load Balancing load balancer] is a valid target (route53-alias-target-elb-answer).
**Route 53 follows.** [Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own] and answers [DNS queries with the new IP address] (route53-alias-follows-resource-ip-changes).
**The client connects.** The user's browser reaches a current node of the load balancer.
plan.table: Alias record targets and what each needs (columns: Target | What must be true): load balancer | [ELB Classic, Application, or Network Load Balancer] (route53-elb-alias-load-balancer-types); CloudFront distribution | the distribution [must include an alternate domain name] that matches (route53-cloudfront-needs-matching-alternate-domain-name), in public zones: [only for public hosted zones] (route53-cloudfront-alias-public-hosted-zones-only); S3 website | [The bucket must have the same name] as the record (route53-s3-website-bucket-name-must-match); API Gateway | the API [has a custom domain name] that matches (route53-api-gateway-needs-matching-custom-domain-name); EC2 instance | an A record with an Elastic IP address, which [will never change] (route53-ec2-elastic-ip-recommended).
plan.why: Why name the resource? AWS moves the addresses of managed resources as they scale; the load balancer's own DNS entry exists so that its [IP addresses can be remapped quickly] (elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap), and an alias record keeps that benefit at your own domain name.
plan.exam_signal: "use a custom domain name for the load balancer" points to an alias record: [create an alias record] (elb-custom-domain-route53-alias); "serve an S3 static website over HTTPS at the company's domain" points to CloudFront in front, because the website endpoint [doesn't support SSL/TLS] (route53-s3-website-endpoint-no-https).
plan.spot_the_bug: An alias record for www.example.com points to the S3 website endpoint of a bucket named example-www-site, and the browser gets an error. Reveal: the bucket name must be www.example.com, because [The bucket must have the same name] as the domain or subdomain (route53-s3-website-bucket-name-must-match). About 60 words with the reveal.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: point the name at the load balancer with an alias record, and Route 53 follows its addresses. The thing to watch is any copy of the addresses in an A record.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team moves its site from an Application Load Balancer to a CloudFront distribution and changes the alias record to the distribution. Requests for the custom name now fail at CloudFront. What is missing? Answer: the distribution [must include an alternate domain name] that matches the record name (route53-cloudfront-needs-matching-alternate-domain-name).

sections.heading: Resolvers cache each answer for its TTL before they ask Route 53 again

plan.problem: A team changes the address of www.example.com at noon. In the afternoon, some users still reach the old server.
trace: **Change.** [Changes generally propagate to all Route 53 servers] [within 60 seconds] (route53-changes-propagate-within-60-seconds).

**Cached answers stay.** A resolver keeps a record for its TTL, the [amount of time, in seconds] that it caches the values (route53-ttl-defined). Caching resolvers are outside Route 53's control and cache records [according to their time to live (TTL)] (route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control).
**Expire and ask again.** When the TTL ends, the resolver asks Route 53 again and gets the new value.

**Plan the change.** Before you change critical records, [temporarily shorten the TTLs] (route53-best-practice-shorten-ttl-before-critical-change), wait for the old TTL to pass, then change the value.
plan.table: The TTL trade-off (columns: TTL | Cost | A change reaches users): long | [A longer TTL reduces your Route 53 charges] (route53-ttl-longer-cheaper-shorter-faster-change) | after the long TTL; short | more queries to pay for | soon: [A shorter TTL reduces the time] (same fact); record with a health check | AWS recommends [60 seconds or less] (route53-ttl-health-check-60-seconds-or-less) | soon after a failover.
plan.why: Why cache at all? The cache lets the resolver [respond more quickly the next time] (route53-resolver-caches-answer-for-ttl-you-set), and fewer queries reach Route 53, where they cost money.
plan.exam_signal: "users still reach the old server after a DNS change" points to the TTL of the old record: [temporarily shorten the TTLs] before the change (route53-best-practice-shorten-ttl-before-critical-change); "records used for DNS failover" points to a short TTL: [60 seconds or less] (route53-rel10-failover-records-short-ttl).
plan.startup_example: Story, at most 60 words with the label, no number: Ben lowers the TTL of Callvale's records at the registrar before the move to Route 53, so that the switch reaches users quickly. The reason is in the trace; the callout states no AWS rule.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: moving a live domain to Route 53. Create a hosted zone with [the same name as your domain] and recreate the records (route53-migrate-in-use-recreate-records-in-new-zone), or import a zone file (route53-migrate-in-use-zone-file-import). Set the NS record TTL to [a value between 60 seconds and 900 seconds] and wait [two days after you lowered the TTL] (route53-migrate-lower-ns-ttl-60-to-900-wait-two-days); then change the name servers at the registrar, and if traffic stops, change them [back to the previous name servers] (route53-migrate-in-use-monitor-and-switch-back). At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a DNS change reaches a user when that user's resolver cache expires. The thing to watch is the old TTL, so lower it well before the change.
plan.stop_and_answer: A record has a TTL of 86400 seconds. At 10:00 a team lowers it to 60 seconds and at 10:05 changes the address. A resolver cached the record at 09:00. When does it see the new address? Answer: when its cached copy runs out, a full old TTL after 09:00: it caches records [according to their time to live (TTL)] (route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control) that it got, so the lower TTL helps only after the old one has run out. The prompt numbers are example values; the reveal names no computed time with a unit.

sections.heading: Weighted records give each resource its share of the total weight

plan.problem: A team releases a new version of its application and wants a small share of users to reach it first.
trace: **Create a group.** You create [records with the same name and type] for each resource (route53-weighted-routing-share-of-total-weight), each with a weight [between 0 and 255] (route53-weighted-weight-range-0-255).
**Add up.** Route 53 adds the weights and answers in the [ratio of a resource's weight to the total] (route53-weighted-ratio-of-weight-to-total).
**Answer.** With weights 3 and 1, the first record comes back [75% of the time] and the second [25% of the time] (route53-faq-wrr-weight-3-and-1-gives-75-25).
**Shift or stop.** Change the weights step by step; to stop traffic to one resource, [change the weight for that record to 0] (route53-weighted-routing-weight-zero-stops-traffic).
plan.table: Three ways to spread answers (columns: Policy | What Route 53 returns | Health checks): simple | one record; with several values, all of them [to the recursive resolver in random order] (route53-simple-routing-multiple-values-random-order-no-health-check) | none: [they are not health checked] (same fact); weighted | one record, chosen by its share of the weight | one per record, optional; multivalue answer | [up to eight healthy records] (route53-multivalue-up-to-eight-healthy) | one per record; a record without one [always considers the record to be healthy] (route53-multivalue-no-health-check-always-healthy).
plan.why: Why weights? You decide the share, so a new version can be tested with few users first: weighted routing helps with [testing new versions of software] (route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions).
plan.exam_signal: "send a small share of users to a new version" or "A/B testing" points to weighted records ([A/B testing], route53-faq-wrr-weights-set-frequency); "return several healthy IP addresses at random" points to multivalue answer records ([up to eight healthy records selected at random], route53-choose-multivalue-routing-up-to-eight-healthy).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: if every weight in the group is 0, traffic goes to all resources with [equal probability] (route53-weighted-all-zero-equal-probability).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: weights set each resource's share of the answers. The thing to watch is a weight of zero, which can still get users when the other records are unhealthy.
plan.stop_and_answer: Records A and B have weights 4 and 0, and both have health checks. A becomes unhealthy. Does Route 53 send users to B? Answer: yes; when all records with a weight above 0 are unhealthy, Route 53 [considers the zero-weighted records] (route53-weighted-zero-weight-used-when-all-unhealthy).

sections.heading: Latency records follow measured latency and geolocation records follow user location

plan.problem: A company runs the same application in two Regions. Most users should reach the faster Region, but users in one market must stay with the Region that holds their data.
trace: **Locate the user.** Route 53 sees the resolver, not the user. It uses [the source IP address of the DNS resolver] (route53-edns0-without-support-uses-resolver-ip), or [a shortened version of the user's IP address] when the resolver sends one (route53-edns0-with-support-uses-user-subnet).

**Latency records.** Route 53 finds which [Region gives the user the lowest latency] among the Regions with a record (route53-latency-routing-lowest-latency-region), from [latency data taken over a period of time] (route53-latency-changes-over-time).

**Geolocation records.** Route 53 matches the location [by continent, by country, or by state] (route53-geolocation-location-levels); for overlapping records, [priority goes to the smallest geographic region] (route53-geolocation-smallest-region-wins).

**No match.** A default record [handles both queries from unmapped IP addresses] and other places (route53-geolocation-default-record-handles-unmapped); without one, Route 53 [returns a "no answer" response] (route53-geolocation-no-default-no-answer).
plan.table: Three kinds of near (columns: Policy | Chooses by | Use it for): latency | [the Region that provides the best latency] (route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region) | speed: [we recommend using Latency Based Routing] (route53-faq-lbr-for-latency-geo-for-compliance); geolocation | [based on the location of your users] (route53-choose-geolocation-routing-user-location) | compliance and language: [we recommend using Geo DNS] (same fact), limits to [only the locations where you have distribution rights] (route53-geolocation-use-cases); geoproximity | where users and resources are, with a bias: [A bias expands or shrinks the geographic region] (route53-geoproximity-bias-expands-or-shrinks-region) | moving traffic between Regions: [shift traffic from resources in one location] (route53-choose-geoproximity-routing-resource-location-bias).
plan.why: Why not use location for speed? Geolocation decides by the [geographic location of the requests] (route53-faq-geo-vs-latency-geography-not-latency); AWS says geography is a good proxy for latency in some cases and not in others, so speed needs measured latency.
plan.exam_signal: "route users to the Region with the lowest latency" points to latency records: [To minimize application latency, use latency-based routing] (route53-bp-latency-for-performance-geo-for-predictability); "users in a specific country" or "distribution rights" points to geolocation records with a default record: [always set a default] (route53-best-practice-always-set-default-record).
plan.diagram: route53-policy-ladder after the table (text fixed in diagrams below).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: geoproximity bias and IP-based routing. A positive bias [from 1 to 99] expands a resource's area and a negative bias of [-1 to -99] shrinks it (route53-geoproximity-bias-positive-range, route53-geoproximity-bias-negative-range); [change the bias in small steps] (route53-geoproximity-change-bias-in-small-steps). For AWS resources you give the [AWS Region or Local Zone Group] (route53-geoproximity-aws-resource-location). IP-based routing uses [the IP addresses that the traffic originates from] (route53-choose-ip-based-routing-known-client-ips), for example users [from certain ISPs to specific endpoints] (route53-ip-based-routing-use-cases). At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: latency records follow network speed, and geolocation records follow where the user is. The thing to watch is the default record for places you did not list.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company has latency records in two Regions. A user in Lisbon reached one Region last week and the other Region this week. Is something broken? Answer: no; latency-based routing uses [latency data taken over a period of time] (route53-latency-changes-over-time), and latency between hosts changes, so the best Region can change too.

sections.heading: Health checkers around the world decide whether an endpoint is healthy

plan.problem: One web server stops answering. Route 53 needs evidence before it changes any answer, and one failed request from one place is not enough.
trace: **Send requests.** At regular intervals Route 53 sends [automated requests over the internet] (route53-hc-endpoint-automated-requests-over-internet): [an HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP request] to [the IP address and port that you specified] (route53-hc-request-types-http-https-tcp-to-ip-and-port), by default every [30 seconds] (route53-hc-request-interval-default-30).

**Judge one response.** An HTTP check [waits for an HTTP status code of 2xx or 3xx] (route53-hc-http-https-status-2xx-3xx); the connection must open [within four seconds] (route53-hc-http-tcp-connect-four-seconds).
**Count failures.** A checker marks the endpoint unhealthy after the failure threshold of consecutive failures, by default [three health checks] (route53-hc-failure-threshold-default-3).
**Combine the checkers.** The endpoint is healthy if [more than 18%] of the health checkers report it healthy (route53-hc-healthy-above-18-percent).
plan.table: Kinds of health checks (columns: Kind | Watches | Use it when): endpoint | an endpoint given [either by IP address or by domain name] (route53-hc-endpoint-by-ip-or-domain) | the resource is reachable from the internet; calculated | it [monitors whether Route 53 considers other health checks healthy or unhealthy] (route53-hc-calculated-monitors-other-health-checks) | you care about [when a specified number of resources] fail (route53-health-check-can-monitor-other-health-checks-two-of-five); CloudWatch alarm | the data [based on the data stream for the alarm] (route53-hc-private-endpoint-cloudwatch-alarm-health-check) | the resource has only private addresses, or a metric decides.
plan.why: Why many checkers and a low bar? The [18% value was chosen] (route53-hc-18-percent-why-chosen) so that checkers in several Regions must agree, and a network problem near a few checkers does not mark a working endpoint unhealthy.
plan.exam_signal: "the instances have only private IP addresses" points to a health check on a CloudWatch alarm (route53-hc-private-endpoint-cloudwatch-alarm-health-check: [CloudWatch metric, associate an alarm with the metric]); "notify the team when the site is unhealthy" points to a health check alarm: [Route 53 sets a CloudWatch alarm] and [CloudWatch uses Amazon SNS to notify users] (route53-health-check-notification-uses-cloudwatch-and-sns).
plan.spot_the_bug: The health check of the primary failover record uses the domain name www.example.com, which is the name of the failover records themselves, and the results change from minute to minute. Reveal: give the domain name of each server, not the record name, or [health check results will be unpredictable] (route53-hc-domain-name-not-record-name). About 60 words with the reveal.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: checkers in many places test the endpoint, and enough of them must agree. The thing to watch is your firewall, which must let the checkers in.
plan.stop_and_answer: An HTTPS health check targets a server whose certificate expired yesterday. The page still returns status 200. Is the endpoint healthy? Answer: yes; HTTPS checks [don't validate SSL/TLS certificates] (route53-hc-https-does-not-validate-certificates), so the check passes.

sections.heading: Route 53 leaves unhealthy records out of answers until every record is unhealthy

plan.problem: A name has three weighted records, one for each server, and one server fails. Route 53 should stop giving out that address, but it must still answer.
trace: **Choose among records.** A health check matters when Route 53 is [choosing between two or more records] — use the display 'useful only when Route 53 is choosing between two or more records' (route53-health-check-useful-only-when-choosing-between-records).
**Skip the unhealthy.** When a health check finds its resource unhealthy, [Route 53 routes traffic away from the associated record] (route53-dns-failover-routes-traffic-away-from-unhealthy-record).
**No check, no doubt.** A record without a health check: Route 53 [always considers it healthy] (route53-record-without-health-check-always-healthy).
**Last resort.** If no record is healthy, Route 53 [considers all the records in the group] healthy and picks one by the routing policy (route53-no-record-healthy-all-records-considered-healthy).
plan.table: Truth table (columns: Records of the name | Health check results | Route 53 answers with): A, B, C, each with a health check | A unhealthy | B or C; A and B with health checks, C without | A and B unhealthy | C; A, B, C, each with a health check | all unhealthy | any of them, by the routing policy.
plan.why: Why answer when everything fails? Route 53 can only fail over to a healthy endpoint, so with none left it will [behave as if all health checks are passing] (route53-faq-all-endpoints-unhealthy-acts-as-all-pass) and returns an answer, not [returning an NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain) response] (route53-last-resort-mode-all-unhealthy-returns-answer).
plan.exam_signal: "an alias record for a load balancer must stop answering when the load balancer has no healthy targets" points to Evaluate Target Health: [set Evaluate Target Health to Yes] (route53-alias-to-aws-use-evaluate-target-health-not-health-check); "a Route 53 health check replaces instances" is wrong: Route 53 changes answers, Elastic Load Balancing [stops sending traffic to it] and EC2 Auto Scaling replaces it (ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace; display 'Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it').
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Route 53 drops unhealthy records but still answers when all of them are unhealthy. The thing to watch is a record with no health check, which counts as healthy.
plan.stop_and_answer: A weighted alias record points to an Application Load Balancer, with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes, and every target behind that load balancer fails. A second weighted record points to a healthy load balancer in another Region. Which load balancer do users get? Answer: the healthy one; with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes, Route 53 can [route traffic away from unhealthy resources] (route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk).

sections.heading: Failover records answer with the secondary only while the primary is unhealthy

plan.problem: A company's application runs in one Region. A static copy of the site in an S3 bucket should take over only when the application fails.
trace: **Two records.** You create [one primary and one secondary failover record] (route53-failover-needs-one-primary-one-secondary) with the same name and type.

**Watch the primary.** For a load balancer, make the primary an alias record and set the [“Evaluate Target Health” parameter to true] (route53-faq-elb-failover-alias-evaluate-target-health); for other endpoints, associate a health check (route53-simple-config-alias-targets-no-health-check-needed: [record and a health check for each resource]).

**Fail over.** While the primary is healthy, Route 53 [responds to DNS queries using the primary record]; when it is unhealthy, it [responds to DNS queries using the secondary record] (route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy).
**Fail back.** When the endpoint passes its health checks again, Route 53 restores it with [no action required on your part] (route53-faq-failback-automatic-after-threshold).
plan.table: Failover outcomes (columns: Primary | Secondary | Route 53 answers with): healthy | any | primary; unhealthy | healthy, or without a health check ([adding a health check is optional], route53-failover-secondary-health-check-optional) | secondary; unhealthy | unhealthy, with a health check | primary: [Route 53 returns the primary record] (route53-failover-both-unhealthy-returns-primary).
plan.why: Why a separate policy? In active-passive failover the secondary is a [group of resources to be on standby] (route53-active-passive-failover-definition), so Route 53 must keep it out of the answers while the primary works; the failover policy is how you [configure active-passive failover] (route53-choose-failover-routing-active-passive).
plan.exam_signal: "active-passive", "a standby site" or "a static maintenance page" points to failover records: you can [maintain a backup site] (route53-faq-failover-backup-site-s3); "both Regions serve users" (active-active) points to latency or weighted records with health checks, for [all of your resources to be available] (route53-active-active-use-all-resources-available).
plan.try_it: route53-t03: one 'Try it' callout after the Exam trap.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: failover records send users to the standby while the main site fails its health checks. The thing to watch is the standby's capacity, because Route 53 does not check load.
plan.stop_and_answer: The primary failover record is an alias record for three weighted records, one for each server, with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes. Two of the three servers fail. Does Route 53 answer with the secondary? Answer: no; the primary counts as healthy while [at least one of the associated resources] is healthy (route53-failover-multiple-primary-healthy-if-one-healthy), and Route 53 [does not make routing decisions] based on load (route53-faq-failover-ignores-endpoint-load), so the last server must carry the traffic.

sections.heading: A private hosted zone answers only through the VPC Resolver of its associated VPCs

plan.problem: A company wants names such as db.corp.internal for its databases. The names must work inside its VPCs and must not be visible on the internet.
trace: **Create and associate.** A private hosted zone holds answers for [DNS queries for a domain and its subdomains] [within one or more VPCs] (route53-private-hosted-zone-defined); you [specify the VPC that you want to associate] when you create it (route53-phz-create-with-one-vpc-associate-more-later).
**Turn on DNS in the VPC.** The VPC [must set both the `enableDnsHostnames` and `enableDnsSupport` attributes to `true`] (vpc-dns-attributes-required-for-private-hosted-zones).

**Query.** An instance asks Route 53 VPC Resolver at the VPC base address [plus two] or at [169.254.169.253] (vpc-dns-resolver-addresses); VPC Resolver [is available by default in all VPCs] (route53-vpc-resolver-recursive-by-default-in-all-vpcs).
**Match the zone.** If a private zone matches the name, VPC Resolver answers from it; if none matches, it [forwards the request to a public DNS resolver] (route53-no-matching-phz-goes-public).
plan.table: Truth table for a VPC associated with private zones (columns: The instance asks for | Private zones | Answer): db.corp.internal | corp.internal has the record | the private record; www.example.com | no private zone matches | the public answer (route53-no-matching-phz-goes-public); api.example.com | a private zone example.com exists without an api record | NXDOMAIN: VPC Resolver [doesn't forward the request to a public DNS] (route53-matching-phz-no-record-returns-nxdomain).
plan.why: Why can the internet not see it? The name servers of a private zone are [reserved and never used by Route 53 public hosted zones] (route53-phz-reserved-ns-not-reachable-from-internet), so the records stay [without exposing DNS data to the public Internet] (route53-features-traffic-flow-and-failover-and-private-dns).
plan.exam_signal: "the same domain name must resolve to internal addresses inside the VPC and public addresses outside" points to split-view DNS with public and [private hosted zones that have the same name] (route53-split-view-dns-definition); "a VPC in another AWS account must use the private hosted zone" points to an association that [you first must authorize], with the CLI or API, because [you can't use the AWS console] (route53-cross-account-association-needs-authorization-no-console).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: policies, Regions and accounts. Private zones support most routing policies, but you [cannot use IP-based routing policy for records] there (route53-phz-routing-policy-support). Latency answers use [the AWS Region of the VPC] that asked (route53-latency-private-zone-uses-vpc-region). One zone can serve [300 Amazon VPCs] (route53-quota-vpcs-per-private-zone), also [VPCs belonging to different accounts] (route53-faq-phz-cross-account-vpcs); VPCs in other Regions get answers in [every VPC that you associate] but need their own connectivity (route53-faq-phz-across-regions-needs-connectivity). At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a private hosted zone answers inside the VPCs that you associate with it. The thing to watch is a private zone that matches a name but has no record for it.
plan.stop_and_answer: A data center server, connected by Site-to-Site VPN, queries the name servers of a private hosted zone over the internet. Does it get the private record? Answer: no; the private zone's records are not returned if you [directly query the name servers over the internet] (route53-phz-reserved-ns-not-reachable-from-internet); the data center needs an inbound endpoint, which the next subsection shows.

sections.heading: Resolver endpoints carry DNS queries between a VPC and an on-premises network

plan.problem: Servers in the data center must resolve names in a private hosted zone, and instances in the VPC must resolve names that only the data center's DNS servers know.
trace: **Connect privately.** Endpoint addresses [aren't public IP addresses] (route53-resolver-inbound-ips-not-public-need-private-link), so the networks are joined by [either Direct Connect or AWS Site-to-Site VPN] (route53-resolver-outbound-path-private-connection).

**Inbound.** An inbound endpoint lets DNS queries reach the VPC [from your on-premises network or another VPC] (route53-resolver-inbound-endpoint-definition); data center DNS servers forward the private zone's domain to the endpoint's addresses.

**Outbound.** An outbound endpoint sends queries [from your VPC to your on-premises network] (route53-resolver-outbound-endpoint-definition), but only for domains that a forwarding rule names: rules decide [which queries VPC Resolver answers itself] (route53-resolver-rules-control-forwarding).
**Most specific wins.** If a query matches several rules, VPC Resolver [chooses the rule with the most specific match] (route53-resolver-rule-most-specific-match-wins).
plan.table: Which endpoint (columns: The query | Endpoint | What you configure): the data center asks for a private zone name | inbound | data center DNS forwards that domain to the endpoint addresses; a VPC instance asks for a data center name | outbound | a forwarding rule for that domain, associated with the VPC; many VPCs and accounts need the same rule | one outbound endpoint | share the rule with AWS RAM: you [need only one outbound endpoint for multiple VPCs] (route53-hybrid-one-outbound-endpoint-shared-by-rules).
plan.why: Why endpoints and not your own DNS servers? Endpoints and rules forward queries [without having to deploy additional DNS servers] (route53-hybrid-resolver-endpoints-no-extra-dns-servers), so there are no forwarder instances to patch and scale.
plan.exam_signal: "on-premises servers must resolve records in a private hosted zone" points to an inbound endpoint; "instances must resolve names that are hosted on premises" points to an outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule: [conditional forwarding rules and Resolver endpoints] (route53-faq-vpc-resolver-hybrid-forwarding-direct-connect-vpn).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: forwarding from the data center straight to the VPC plus-two address [is not supported, and can cause unstable results] (route53-resolver-cidr-plus-two-forwarding-unsupported). Name rule for this subsection: first use 'Route 53 VPC Resolver (formerly Route 53 Resolver)', then 'VPC Resolver'; the former name appears once only (RULINGS hard rule 6).
plan.diagram: route53-hybrid-endpoints after the trace (text fixed in diagrams below).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: DNS Firewall and Profiles. [DNS Firewall is a feature of Route 53 VPC Resolver] (route53-dnsfw-feature-of-vpc-resolver-no-extra-setup) that can [filter and regulate outbound DNS traffic] (route53-dnsfw-filters-outbound-dns-for-vpc) to [help prevent DNS exfiltration of your data] (route53-dns-firewall-blocks-dns-exfiltration); a rule can allow, or [block, or alert on matching queries] (route53-dnsfw-rule-actions-allow-block-alert). Network Firewall [does not have visibility into queries made by Route 53 VPC Resolver] (route53-dns-firewall-vs-network-firewall). Route 53 Profiles apply DNS settings [across many VPCs and in different AWS accounts] (route53-profiles-share-dns-config-across-vpcs-accounts). At most 80 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: inbound endpoints bring the data center's questions in, and outbound endpoints send the VPC's questions out. The thing to watch is the forwarding rule, which decides what goes out.
plan.stop_and_answer: A VPC has a private hosted zone corp.example and also a forwarding rule for corp.example that targets the data center's DNS servers. Where do queries for app.corp.example go? Answer: to the data center; when a private zone and a forwarding rule have the same domain name, [the VPC Resolver rule takes precedence] (route53-resolver-rule-beats-phz-same-name).

sections.heading: DNS answers and health check failover keep working when the control plane is impaired

plan.problem: A company plans for the loss of its main Region. The recovery plan says: if us-east-1 fails, edit the DNS records so that they point to us-west-2.
trace: **Two planes.** For DNS and health checks the [control plane is located in the us-east-1 AWS Region] and the [data planes are globally distributed] (route53-control-plane-us-east-1).

**What each does.** The control plane is the set of APIs that create and change zones, records and health checks ([It is hosted in us-east-1], route53-fi-control-plane-apis-hosted-us-east-1); the data plane answers queries from [over 200 Points of Presence (PoP) locations] (route53-dns-data-plane-pops).

**During an impairment.** [CRUDL-type operations for Route 53 may not work], but DNS resolution, health checks and the routing changes they cause [will continue to work] (route53-fi-impairment-dns-and-health-checks-keep-working).
**So prepare.** Create the failover records and health checks before the event, and fail over on the [status of health checks to perform failovers] (route53-fi-no-control-plane-in-recovery-path).
plan.table: Recovery actions (columns: Action | Plane | Works while the control plane is impaired): a health check fails and failover records switch | data plane | yes: a [highly reliable operation done on the data plane] (route53-dr-health-check-failover-data-plane); change a record or the weights | control plane | maybe not: [this is a control plane operation] (route53-dr-weight-change-is-control-plane); create records for the standby Region during the event | control plane | maybe not; [pre-provision resources that require DNS records] (route53-fi-preprovision-for-multi-region-dr).
plan.why: Why two designs? The control plane is [optimized for data consistency] and the data plane is [optimized for availability] (route53-control-vs-data-plane-design), so the part that answers users is the part built to stay up.
plan.exam_signal: "fail over to another Region even if the Route 53 API is unavailable" points to failover records with health checks created in advance: [use only data plane operations] (route53-dr-failover-use-data-plane-only); "failover must not wait for DNS caches" or "static IP addresses" points to AWS Global Accelerator: [Change propagation takes a matter of seconds] (route53-vs-ga-change-propagation-seconds) and it [avoids caching issues that can occur with DNS] (route53-vs-ga-dr-avoids-dns-caching).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: since 2025-11-26, accelerated recovery for public hosted zones keeps a copy in the [US West (Oregon) Region] and targets a [60-minute Recovery Time Objective (RTO)] for making changes again (route53-accelerated-recovery-60-minute-rto); you [must turn on accelerated recovery before any issues] (route53-accelerated-recovery-turn-on-before-impairment). The Changed recently entry in 1-fast.md carries the change; do not let a question key on it.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: create failover records and health checks before the outage, because they keep working. The thing to watch is any recovery step that edits records during the outage.
plan.stop_and_answer: During a control plane impairment in us-east-1, failover to us-west-2 has worked. The team now wants to add records for a third Region. Can it count on doing that during the event? Answer: no; while the control plane is impaired, [CRUDL-type operations for Route 53 may not work] (route53-fi-impairment-dns-and-health-checks-keep-working), and creating records is one of them.

sections.heading: FAQ quick-fire
sections.plan: Ten 'FAQ <n>.' prompts (see faq), each answered in one clause in its reveal and followed by an AWS quote block of whole sentences from the fact's evidence quote. At most 450 words.

traps.belief: You can point the bare domain, such as example.com, to a load balancer or a CloudFront distribution with a CNAME record.
traps.truth: The DNS protocol does not allow a CNAME record at the zone apex; an alias record can sit there and point to the AWS resource.

traps.belief: An A record with the load balancer's current IP addresses works as well as an alias record.
traps.truth: Elastic Load Balancing remaps the load balancer's addresses as it scales (its DNS entry has a TTL of 60 seconds); an alias record names the load balancer, and Route 53 follows the address changes by itself.

traps.belief: When you change a record, every user gets the new value within a minute.
traps.truth: Route 53 updates its own servers within 60 seconds, but caching resolvers are outside its control and keep the old answer until its TTL runs out.

traps.belief: To send each user to the fastest Region, use geolocation routing.
traps.truth: Latency-based routing picks the Region with the lowest measured latency; geolocation routing decides by the location of the query, which is not always a good proxy for latency, and suits compliance and localization.

traps.belief: A user from a place that has no geolocation record gets the record of the nearest place.
traps.truth: Without a default geolocation record, Route 53 returns a no answer response for places without a record and for IP addresses it cannot map to a location.

traps.belief: Multivalue answer routing with health checks can replace a load balancer.
traps.truth: Multivalue answer routing returns up to eight healthy records at random, and AWS says it is not a substitute for a load balancer.

traps.belief: When every record of a name fails its health check, Route 53 returns no answer.
traps.truth: When no record is healthy, Route 53 considers all of them healthy and answers by the routing policy; with two unhealthy failover records it returns the primary.

traps.belief: Once a name uses health checks, a record without a health check is left out of the answers.
traps.truth: Route 53 always considers a record without a health check healthy and always includes it among the possible answers.

traps.belief: A Route 53 health check can test an instance by its private IP address, because the checkers run inside AWS.
traps.truth: Route 53 cannot check endpoints in private IP ranges, because the health checkers are outside the VPC; for a private resource, create a CloudWatch metric and alarm and a health check on the alarm.

traps.belief: A failover alias record for a load balancer needs its own Route 53 health check of the load balancer.
traps.truth: For an alias record to an AWS resource such as a load balancer, set Evaluate Target Health to Yes; AWS says you should not create Route 53 health checks for those resources.

traps.belief: A Route 53 health check replaces or repairs an instance that fails.
traps.truth: A Route 53 health check changes DNS answers; a load balancer stops sending requests to an unhealthy target, and EC2 Auto Scaling replaces an unhealthy instance.

traps.belief: If a private hosted zone has no record for a name, VPC Resolver asks the public zone of the same name instead.
traps.truth: When a private hosted zone matches the name but has no record for it, VPC Resolver does not forward the query to public DNS; it returns NXDOMAIN.

traps.belief: During a Regional outage, you fail over by editing records or changing weights in Route 53.
traps.truth: Editing records and changing weights depend on the Route 53 control plane in us-east-1, which may not work during an impairment; failover records with health checks, created in advance, run on the data plane and keep working.

traps.belief: Either kind of Resolver endpoint carries DNS queries in both directions between a VPC and the data center.
traps.truth: Inbound Resolver endpoints allow DNS queries into the VPC from the on-premises network; outbound Resolver endpoints, with forwarding rules, allow DNS queries from the VPC to the on-premises network.

traps.belief: On-premises DNS servers can forward queries for a private hosted zone to the VPC CIDR+2 address.
traps.truth: Forwarding private DNS queries from on-premises DNS servers to the VPC CIDR+2 address is not supported and can cause unstable results; use a Resolver inbound endpoint.

traps.belief: With a geolocation record for every continent, every user gets an answer.
traps.truth: Some IP addresses are not mapped to a location; without a default geolocation record, Route 53 returns a no answer response for them.

traps.belief: You can add a record of another routing policy, such as a latency record, beside the records of a name to fill the gaps.
traps.truth: You cannot create non-latency records with the same name and type as latency records, or non-failover records beside failover records; to combine policies, build a tree of alias records.

traps.belief: Evaluate Target Health can watch the health of any record, also an A record with the IP address of an instance.
traps.truth: Evaluate Target Health checks the resource that an alias record refers to; for resources without alias records, such as EC2 instances, you create a record and a health check for each resource.

traps.belief: A health check on the secondary failover record makes Route 53 switch to the secondary when the primary fails.
traps.truth: Route 53 answers with the secondary record when the primary is unhealthy, so the primary record needs the health check or Evaluate Target Health; a record without a health check is considered healthy.

traps.belief: A private hosted zone also answers DNS queries from users on the internet.
traps.truth: A private hosted zone returns its records only when queried from within the VPCs associated with it, or through an inbound endpoint; internet users need a public hosted zone.

traps.belief: To use Route 53 as the DNS service of a domain, you must first transfer the domain registration to Route 53.
traps.truth: A transfer is not required to use other Route 53 features: create a public hosted zone and update the name servers of the domain at the current registrar.

question_slots.note: A company hosts example.com in a Route 53 public hosted zone; its website runs behind an Application Load Balancer; users must open the site at example.com, with no www. Which record meets these requirements? Qualifier none (difficulty 1). Key: an alias record of type A at example.com that points to the load balancer (route53-alias-allowed-at-zone-apex, route53-elb-alias-record-for-root-and-subdomains, route53-faq-apex-alias-elb-three-types). Distractors: a CNAME record at example.com with the load balancer's DNS name (trap route53-trap-cname-at-apex; impossible-feature, why links route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex); an A record with the load balancer's current IP addresses (trap route53-trap-a-record-to-lb-ip; why links route53-elb-dns-entry-updated-ttl-60); an NS record at example.com that names the load balancer (keyword-bait; misconception: an NS record [identifies the name servers for the hosted zone], route53-ns-record-identifies-name-servers). Think-aloud with wrong_path: step 3 predicts 'a CNAME record to the load balancer's DNS name, because a CNAME record maps one name to another'; step 5 'My first idea breaks because example.com is the zone apex, where the DNS protocol does not allow a CNAME record.'

app.example.com is an A record with the IP addresses of an Application Load Balancer, copied when the load balancer was created. Users report intermittent connection errors, mostly after traffic peaks. MOST cost-effective fix. Key: replace the A record with an alias record that points to the load balancer (route53-alias-follows-resource-ip-changes, route53-elb-dns-entry-updated-ttl-60, route53-pricing-alias-free-for-listed-aws-services). Distractors: a CNAME record for app.example.com with the load balancer's DNS name (violates-qualifier: it works, but Route 53 [charges for CNAME queries], route53-alias-queries-free-cname-charged); a scheduled Lambda function that rewrites the A record with the current addresses every minute (violates-qualifier; misconception: answers stay cached for the TTL); attach Elastic IP addresses to the Application Load Balancer and keep the A record (trap elb-trap-alb-static-ip; impossible-feature, why links elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only). The subdomain allows a CNAME record, so the qualifier, not the apex rule, decides.

A company will migrate www.example.com from servers in its data center to an Application Load Balancer next Saturday. The current Route 53 record is an A record with a TTL of 86,400 seconds. Users must switch with minimal downtime, and the company must be able to roll back quickly. Which approach will move users with the LEAST downtime? Key: at least one day before Saturday, lower the TTL of the A record to 60 seconds; on Saturday, replace it with an alias record for the load balancer (route53-best-practice-shorten-ttl-before-critical-change, route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control, route53-ttl-start-shorter-300-seconds-in-use). Distractors: change the record on Saturday, because Route 53 propagates changes within 60 seconds (trap route53-trap-ttl-instant-change); on Saturday, lower the TTL and change the value in one change batch (misconception: resolvers keep the old answer for the old TTL; violates-qualifier); create a second hosted zone for example.com with the new record and switch the registrar's name servers on Saturday (misconception: NS records are cached for [172800 seconds], route53-ns-record-typical-ttl-172800; violates-qualifier). The stem numbers are scenario values.

A media company uses geolocation records: users in Europe go to eu-west-1 and users in North America to us-east-1, as its distribution rights require. Users in South America, and some users whose location cannot be identified, get no answer. Those users must be served from us-east-1 with the LEAST operational overhead. Key: add a geolocation record with the location Default that points to us-east-1 (route53-geolocation-default-record-handles-unmapped, route53-geolocation-recommend-one-default-record). Distractors: add one geolocation record for each remaining continent (violates-qualifier, and unmapped addresses still get no answer: route53-geolocation-maps-ip-addresses-some-unmapped); add a latency record with the same name that points to us-east-1 (impossible-feature, why links route53-latency-no-non-latency-record-same-name-type); replace the records with geoproximity records (sibling-confusion: breaks the distribution-rights rule; trap route53-trap-geolocation-no-default does not fit: use a misconception).

Three EC2 instances with Elastic IP addresses serve www.example.com through three weighted A records, each with a Route 53 health check and a nonzero weight. During a failed deployment all three fail, and users still get their addresses. When no instance is healthy, users must get a static error page from an S3 bucket named www.example.com that is configured as a website. LEAST operational overhead. Key: add a fourth weighted record of the same name, an alias record for the S3 website endpoint with a weight of 0 (route53-weighted-zero-weight-health-nonzero-first, route53-weighted-zero-weight-used-when-all-unhealthy, route53-s3-website-bucket-name-must-match). Distractors: rename the weighted records and build failover records whose primary is an alias record for them and whose secondary is the S3 website (violates-qualifier: it works, with more records to change; route53-failover-no-non-failover-record-same-name-type explains the rename); rely on Route 53 to return no answer when every health check fails, and show the error page from the browser (trap route53-trap-all-unhealthy-no-answer); delete the health checks so that Route 53 stops returning failed instances (trap route53-trap-record-without-health-check-skipped). Do not offer Route 53 Profiles or an AWS RAM share as an option: with one VPC the direct association is least overhead, but a Profile is a defensible second answer.

tasks.title: Read the health checker IP ranges and your Route 53 quotas
tasks.kills: "Route 53 health checks run inside my VPC, so they can test private addresses."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, read-only, 3 minutes, $0. 1) aws route53 get-checker-ip-ranges: expect a list of public CIDR ranges; checkers send [automated requests over the internet] (route53-hc-endpoint-automated-requests-over-internet), and Route 53 cannot check addresses in [local, private, nonroutable, or multicast ranges] (route53-hc-cannot-check-private-ip-ranges). 2) aws route53 get-account-limit --type MAX_HEALTH_CHECKS_BY_OWNER: expect the limit and the current count; the default is [200 active health checks] (route53-quota-health-checks-per-account), unless the account has a higher quota. 3) aws route53 get-account-limit --type MAX_HOSTED_ZONES_BY_OWNER: the initial quota is [500 per AWS account] (route53-quota-hosted-zones-per-account). 4) Optional: aws route53 list-hosted-zones (may be empty). Creates nothing. Commands from the official CLI reference pages in the corpus (tasks check-cli --reference); the writer confirms the --type values there. Route 53 is a global service, so the CloudShell Region does not matter for these calls ([Route 53 is a global service], route53-hc-global-service-no-region-for-health-checks).

tasks.title: Point the zone apex at another record after a CNAME record is refused
tasks.kills: "A CNAME record can point the bare domain to another name."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, about 10 minutes. Cost line: a hosted zone deleted within 12 hours is not charged ([deleted within 12 hours of creation], route53-pricing-hosted-zone-deleted-in-12-hours-free); no prices. 1) Create a public hosted zone saa-route53-t02.example with a unique caller reference; capture ZONE_ID (HostedZone.Id). The step text says that no registrar points to this lab zone, so it answers no internet traffic; if the guide or the CLI reference shows that a reserved name is refused, use <DOMAIN>, a subdomain of a domain the reader administers ([a domain that you have permission to administer], route53-migrate-hosted-zone-only-for-domain-you-administer). 2) Tag the zone in the next step (create-hosted-zone takes no tags): aws route53 change-tags-for-resource --resource-type hostedzone --resource-id $ZONE_ID --add-tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=route53-t02. 3) Create an A record www.saa-route53-t02.example with the documentation address 192.0.2.10 and a TTL of 300 seconds. 4) Break it: predict ('Can the apex hold a CNAME record that points to www?'), then try a CNAME record at saa-route53-t02.example with the value www.saa-route53-t02.example; expect an InvalidChangeBatch error; explain: the [DNS protocol does not allow you to create] a CNAME record at the apex (route53-cname-dns-protocol-forbids-zone-apex). 5) Fix: create an alias record of type A at the apex whose target is the www record of the same zone (alias records route [one record in a hosted zone to another], route53-alias-extension-targets), with EvaluateTargetHealth false. 6) aws route53 test-dns-answer --hosted-zone-id $ZONE_ID --record-name saa-route53-t02.example --record-type A: expect 192.0.2.10. Cleanup in reverse order: delete the alias record, delete the www record, delete-hosted-zone. Verify: aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=task,Values=route53-t02 returns nothing (T108) once fr-0078 confirms that the Tagging API lists hosted zones; until then park the verify step and report it, or use the T108 exception with aws route53 list-hosted-zones-by-name --dns-name saa-route53-t02.example. The writer confirms with tasks check-cli --reference the change-batch syntax and that test-dns-answer answers for this zone. Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'.

tasks.title: Watch failover records answer while the primary health check fails
tasks.kills: "When every record fails its health check, Route 53 returns no answer."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, about 15 minutes. Cost line: the hosted zone is not charged if deleted within 12 hours (route53-pricing-hosted-zone-deleted-in-12-hours-free); a calculated health check is billed as a health check of an AWS endpoint (route53-pricing-health-check-aws-vs-non-aws-endpoints), and the first ones are free ([up to 50 health checks for AWS endpoints], route53-pricing-health-checks-first-50-aws-endpoints-free); no prices. 1) Create the lab zone saa-route53-t03.example (same name rule as route53-t02) and tag it. 2) Create a calculated health check with no child health checks and HealthThreshold 1, which is [always considers this health check to be unhealthy] (route53-hc-calculated-threshold-above-children-unhealthy); capture HC_ID; tag it with change-tags-for-resource --resource-type healthcheck. If the CLI reference refuses an empty child list, use HealthThreshold 0 (always healthy, route53-hc-calculated-threshold-zero-always-healthy) with Inverted true (route53-hc-invert-reverses-status) and say so. 3) Create failover records for www: PRIMARY 192.0.2.10 with HealthCheckId $HC_ID; SECONDARY 198.51.100.10 without a health check. 4) test-dns-answer for www: expect 198.51.100.10, the secondary (route53-failover-one-primary-one-secondary-responds-secondary-when-unhealthy). 5) Break it: predict ('If the secondary gets the same unhealthy health check, does Route 53 stop answering?'), add HealthCheckId $HC_ID to the secondary, run test-dns-answer: expect 192.0.2.10; explain: [Route 53 returns the primary record] when both are unhealthy (route53-failover-both-unhealthy-returns-primary). 6) Fix: update the health check so that it is healthy (HealthThreshold 0); expect 192.0.2.10 as the healthy primary. Cleanup in reverse order: delete both records, delete-health-check, delete-hosted-zone. Verify by the tag task=route53-t03 (T108) once fr-0078 is filled; until then park it as in route53-t02. Label 'checked against docs, not run in a real account'.

speak.prompt: Why can I not point an A record at the IP address of the load balancer?
speak.note: Short answer: because those addresses change as the load balancer scales; an alias record names the load balancer, and Route 53 follows the changes. How it works: Elastic Load Balancing updates its own DNS entry with a short TTL; an alias record points to the load balancer itself, so Route 53 answers with whatever addresses are current, and it also works at callvale.example, where a CNAME record is not allowed. Watch: if a customer must allow-list fixed addresses, that needs a Network Load Balancer or AWS Global Accelerator, not an A record. In your case: 'Which of our names go to the load balancer directly, and which go through CloudFront?' Must not say: 'the load balancer's IP addresses never change'; 'use a CNAME record at callvale.example'; 'an alias record is the same as a CNAME record'.

speak.persona: a SaaS founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Latency routing or geolocation routing: which one sends my users to the fastest Region?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both look at where the query comes from, but latency routing picks the fastest Region and geolocation routing picks by country or continent. How it works: latency routing uses measurements between users' networks and AWS Regions, taken over time; geolocation matches the user's location to the records you made, and the smallest area wins. Watch: geolocation needs a default record, or some users get no answer. In your case: 'Do you have a rule that keeps users of one country in one Region?' Must not say: 'geolocation sends each user to the nearest Region'; 'latency routing measures how fast your own servers respond' (latency data is traffic between users and AWS data centers).

speak.prompt: We run in two Regions. If the first Region fails, how does DNS move our users to the second one, and how fast?
speak.note: Short answer: failover records with a health check on the primary; users move once the checks fail and their cached answer runs out, so think minutes, not seconds. How it works: checkers test the primary every thirty seconds by default, three failures in a row make it unhealthy, Route 53 then answers with the secondary, and each resolver asks again when its TTL ends; keep that TTL at sixty seconds or less. Watch: set it all up in advance, because editing records during an outage may not work; if seconds matter, AWS Global Accelerator moves traffic without waiting for DNS caches. In your case: 'How long can your users wait during a failover?' Must not say: 'users move instantly'; 'we update the DNS records when it happens'; 'Route 53 replaces the failed servers'. Numbers as words, from the facts' spoken forms.

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Our domain is registered with another company. Do we have to move it to AWS to use Route 53?
speak.note: Short answer: no; you keep the registration and point the domain at Route 53's name servers. How it works: you create a hosted zone, copy your records into it, and at your registrar you replace the name servers with the four that Route 53 gives the zone. Watch: lower the TTLs a day or two before the switch, so that you can roll back quickly if something is missing. In your case: 'Who in your team can log in to the registrar today?' Must not say: 'you must transfer the domain first'; 'the switch reaches every user within a minute'.

cards.front: In Route 53, the zone apex example.com must point to a load balancer. Which record do you create?
cards.back: An alias record.

cards.front: In Route 53, can you create a CNAME record at the zone apex?
cards.back: No. The DNS protocol does not allow it.

cards.front: In Route 53, each user must reach the Region with the best latency. Which routing policy do you choose?
cards.back: Latency-based routing.

cards.front: Route 53 health check or Elastic Load Balancing health check: which one changes DNS answers?
cards.back: The Route 53 health check.

cards.front: In Route 53, every record of a name is unhealthy. Does Route 53 return no answer?
cards.back: No. It treats all of them as healthy and answers.

cards.front: In Route 53 VPC Resolver, on-premises servers must resolve names in a private hosted zone. What do you create?
cards.back: An inbound Resolver endpoint.

cards.front: In Route 53, each new hosted zone gets {{c1::a unique set of four name servers}}.
In Route 53, AWS recommends a TTL of {{c1::60 seconds or less}} for a record with a health check.
In Route 53, the default request interval of a health check is {{c1::30 seconds}}.
In Route 53, the default failure threshold of a health check is {{c1::three health checks}}.
In Route 53, an endpoint is healthy if {{c1::more than 18%}} of the health checkers report it healthy.
In Route 53, multivalue answer routing returns {{c1::up to eight healthy records}} per query.
In Route 53, the weight of a weighted record is an integer {{c1::between 0 and 255}}.
In Route 53, record changes generally reach all Route 53 servers {{c1::within 60 seconds}}.
In Route 53, users of one country must always be served from one Region for compliance. Which routing policy do you choose?
cards.back: Geolocation routing.

cards.front: In Route 53 geolocation routing with no default record, does a user from an unlisted country get an answer?
cards.back: No. Route 53 returns a no answer response.

cards.front: In Route 53, is multivalue answer routing a substitute for a load balancer?
cards.back: No. It returns healthy addresses; it does not balance load.

cards.front: In Route 53, can a health check test an endpoint by its private IP address?
cards.back: No. Health checkers cannot reach private IP ranges.

cards.front: In Route 53, an instance has only a private IP address. How do you check its health?
cards.back: A health check on a CloudWatch alarm.

cards.front: In Route 53, a failover alias record points to a load balancer. How does it follow the load balancer's health?
cards.back: Set Evaluate Target Health to Yes.

cards.front: In Route 53, you must change a critical record next week. What do you do first?
cards.back: Temporarily shorten the record's TTL.

cards.front: In Route 53, can you set the TTL of an alias record that points to an AWS resource?
cards.back: No. Route 53 uses the resource's default TTL.

cards.front: In Route 53 VPC Resolver, instances must resolve names that on-premises DNS servers host. What do you create?
cards.back: An outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule.

cards.front: In Route 53 VPC Resolver, can on-premises DNS servers forward queries to the VPC plus-two address?
cards.back: No. Not supported; use an inbound endpoint.

cards.front: In Route 53, a private hosted zone matches a name but has no record for it. Does VPC Resolver ask public DNS?
cards.back: No. It returns NXDOMAIN.

cards.front: In Route 53, a small share of users must test a new version. Which routing policy do you choose?
cards.back: Weighted routing.

cards.front: In Route 53, can you use IP-based routing for records in a private hosted zone?
cards.back: No.

cards.front: In Route 53, failover must work while the control plane is impaired. What do you rely on?
cards.back: Health checks and failover records created in advance.

cards.front: In Route 53, the domain stays with another registrar. What must the registrar change?
cards.back: The name servers, to those of the hosted zone.

cards.front: In Amazon S3, can a website endpoint serve your domain over HTTPS?
cards.back: No. Put CloudFront in front of the bucket.

cards.front: Geolocation or geoproximity routing: which one uses a bias?
cards.back: Geoproximity routing.

cards.front: In a VPC, a compromised instance could send data out through DNS lookups. What blocks those queries?
cards.back: DNS Firewall, a feature of Route 53 VPC Resolver.

diagrams.title: One DNS query, from the browser to Route 53
diagrams.claim: A resolver finds the Route 53 name servers through the TLD name server, gets the answer from the hosted zone, and caches it for the TTL.
diagrams.alt: A sequence with four participants: a browser, a DNS resolver, the TLD name server for .com and a Route 53 name server. The browser asks the resolver. The resolver asks the TLD name server, which names the Route 53 name servers. The resolver asks a Route 53 name server, which returns the address from the hosted zone. The resolver returns it to the browser and keeps a copy.
say: The browser asks a DNS resolver, usually run by the internet service provider, for www.example.com.
The resolver asks a sequence of authoritative name servers, starting with the TLD name server for .com.
The TLD name server answers with the names of the four Route 53 name servers of the domain.
A Route 53 name server finds the record in the hosted zone and returns the IP address.
The resolver gives the address to the browser and caches it for the TTL of the record.
diagrams.note: Size s. Four participants left to right: browser (user icon), DNS resolver (plain label), TLD name server for .com (plain label), Route 53 name server (route53 icon, emph). Messages 1 to 5 as numbered arrows; step 5 is the return arrow with a small 'cached for the TTL' note. The root name server is left out: no fact names its step. In the Markdown steps link step 1 to route53-resolver-typically-managed-by-isp, step 2 to route53-dns-resolver-is-recursive-name-server, step 3 to route53-tld-returns-four-name-servers, step 4 to route53-name-server-returns-value-from-hosted-zone, step 5 to route53-ttl-defined. No AWS number in labels or steps ('four' is a small number word).

diagrams.title: Which routing policy?
diagrams.claim: The requirement in the stem decides the routing policy of the records.
diagrams.alt: A decision ladder with five questions. A standby that waits for a failure leads to failover records; users who must stay in a country or area lead to geolocation records; the fastest Region leads to latency records; fixed shares lead to weighted records; several healthy addresses without a load balancer lead to multivalue answer records. Otherwise, a simple record.
rungs: Should a standby wait until the main site fails? -> Failover records
Must users stay inside a country or area? -> Geolocation records (emph)
Should each user get the fastest Region? -> Latency records (emph)
Should traffic split by fixed shares? -> Weighted records
Several healthy addresses without a load balancer? -> Multivalue answer records
diagrams.note: Ladder kind: questions at most 9 words, outcomes at most 4 words; no absolute word and no number with a unit in labels. Geoproximity and IP-based routing are not rungs; the table and the Go deeper block teach them. The caption links route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region and route53-choose-geolocation-routing-user-location.

diagrams.title: DNS between a VPC and a data center
diagrams.claim: Inbound endpoints bring data center queries to VPC Resolver, and outbound endpoints carry VPC queries to the data center's DNS servers when a forwarding rule matches.
diagrams.alt: An architecture with a data center on the left and a VPC on the right, joined by Direct Connect or a VPN. Data center DNS servers forward queries to an inbound endpoint, which reaches VPC Resolver and a private hosted zone. An instance's query goes through VPC Resolver, a forwarding rule and an outbound endpoint back to the data center DNS servers.
say: The data center DNS servers forward queries for the private zone's domain to the inbound endpoint.
VPC Resolver answers them from the private hosted zone.
An instance asks VPC Resolver for a name that the data center hosts.
A forwarding rule matches the name, and the outbound endpoint sends the query to the data center DNS servers.
diagrams.note: Size m, at most 8 nodes: data center DNS servers, Direct Connect or VPN (one link label), inbound endpoint, outbound endpoint, VPC Resolver, private hosted zone, forwarding rule (label on the outbound path), EC2 instance. Two paths: inbound (top, numbered 1 and 2) and outbound (bottom, numbered 3 and 4). Data center on the left (STARTUP A7 rule 13). No port numbers in labels.

diagrams.title: Callvale before: DNS at the registrar
diagrams.claim: The registrar's DNS answers callvale.example with the address of one old instance, so users never reach CloudFront or the load balancer.
diagrams.alt: Before: users on the left ask the registrar's DNS for callvale.example and get the IP address of one old instance. CloudFront and the Application Load Balancer stand on the right with no name that points to them.
say: The registrar's DNS answers with the address of one old instance.
CloudFront and the load balancer are ready, but no name points to them.
diagrams.note: Story picture. Steps are story, not AWS rules: no fact link, no number. Keep each component in the same grid cell as in route53-after (STARTUP A7 rule 13): users on the left, DNS next, the edge (CloudFront), then the load balancer and the web tier.

diagrams.title: Callvale after: alias records in a Route 53 hosted zone
diagrams.claim: The registrar points the domain to the Route 53 hosted zone, whose alias records send both names to CloudFront in front of the load balancer.
diagrams.alt: After: the registrar lists the four name servers of a Route 53 public hosted zone. Alias records for callvale.example and app.callvale.example point to CloudFront, which sends requests to the Application Load Balancer. A health check watches the site and alarms through Amazon SNS.
say: The registrar lists the name servers of the Route 53 hosted zone.
Alias records for callvale.example and app.callvale.example answer with CloudFront addresses.
CloudFront sends requests to the Application Load Balancer.
A health check watches the site, and its alarm notifies the team through Amazon SNS.
diagrams.note: At most 8 nodes: users, registrar, Route 53 hosted zone (route53 icon) with two alias records, CloudFront (cloudfront icon), Application Load Balancer (alb icon), web instances (one group), health check and SNS (one small node each). No second Region (stage 4), no AWS WAF (stage 3). No numbers in labels or steps. Step 3 states no AWS rule; link steps 1, 2 and 4 to their facts.
